clinicalPearls: Characterised by intense pricking or burning itch triggered by contact with water at any temperature, developing within minutes and lasting up to an hour, without any visible rash
The absence of weals distinguishes it from aquagenic urticaria, in which contact with water produces true urticarial lesions
It has an important association with myeloproliferative disorders, especially polycythaemia vera, where water-induced itch may precede diagnosis by years
Other reported associations include myelodysplasia and, occasionally, other systemic disease, so new-onset aquagenic pruritus warrants a search for an underlying cause
The legs are often most affected, and patients frequently learn to limit bathing or dry themselves rapidly to reduce symptoms
Investigation should include a full blood count and, where indicated, further haematological assessment for a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Management is challenging and includes measures such as antihistamines, phototherapy and treatment of any underlying disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Aquagenic pruritus is thought to result from water-triggered activation of cutaneous mast cells and sensory nerves, with release of pruritogenic mediators despite the lack of a visible eruption. In association with myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythaemia vera, abnormal mast cell and basophil activity and increased mediator release are proposed to underlie the itch, and heightened fibrinolytic and neurogenic activity in the skin may contribute. The mechanism in idiopathic cases is less well defined but is presumed to share this neuro-mast-cell pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Polycythaemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms presenting with itch
Cholinergic urticaria triggered by warm water
Cold or heat urticaria depending on water temperature
Xerosis-related or senile pruritus aggravated by bathing
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count to screen for polycythaemia and other haematological abnormality
Water-provocation to confirm the trigger and demonstrate the absence of weals
Haematological assessment including JAK2 testing where a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected
Review for cholestasis, renal impairment and other systemic causes of pruritus
Skin examination to confirm the absence of a primary dermatosis
Iron studies and other tests as guided by the clinical picture
redFlags: A raised haematocrit, splenomegaly or thrombotic history suggesting polycythaemia vera
Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fever or night sweats pointing to systemic disease
Progressive or refractory itch with abnormal blood counts requiring haematology referral
Onset in an older patient with other features of an underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic aquagenic pruritus tends to be chronic and can be difficult to control, though symptoms may fluctuate; when it is a manifestation of a myeloproliferative disorder, the prognosis and treatment are governed by the underlying condition, and effective management of that disorder often improves the itch.
pitfalls: Failing to check a full blood count and thereby missing an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm
Confusing it with aquagenic urticaria despite the absence of weals
Attributing the itch simply to dry skin and overlooking a systemic cause
Not reassessing patients over time, since haematological disease may declare itself later
references: British Association of Dermatologists resources on pruritus
management: Investigate for and treat an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm such as polycythaemia vera, since controlling it often relieves the itch
Offer first-line symptomatic relief with antihistamines
Use skin-directed measures including alkalinisation of bath water with sodium bicarbonate, prompt drying, emollients and reduced water temperature and exposure
Provide narrowband UVB phototherapy for resistant symptoms
Consider add-on neuromodulators such as an SSRI for refractory pruritus
Screen for and correct other systemic causes including cholestasis, renal impairment and iron deficiency
Refer to haematology with ongoing surveillance where a myeloproliferative neoplasm is suspected
